q.young: How many times have you thrown up?
q.older: How many times have you thrown up since you hurt your head?

candidates.why: Item 1 says ask for a count, not yes/no, so one answer serves both PECARN's binary and CHALICE's three-episode threshold.

q.young: Was it none, once, a few times, or lots?
q.older: Roughly how many times: none, once, two, three, or more than three?

candidates.why: Bucketed variant for the packet's open question on count buckets; the older wording keeps the three-episode boundary visible while the young one stays countable.

q.young: Have you thrown up today?
q.older: How many times have you thrown up today, not counting earlier days?

candidates.why: For older injuries a total since the bump is uninformative; anchoring the count to today separates ongoing vomiting from a single early episode.

q.young: Does your head hurt more than it did yesterday?
q.older: Is your head hurting more now than it was yesterday?

candidates.why: Item 2 is a trajectory rather than a snapshot, and yesterday gives the child a concrete point to compare against.

q.young: Does your head hurt more than when you woke up?
q.older: Has your headache got stronger since you woke up this morning?

candidates.why: Same trajectory item with a same-day anchor, which is the only comparison a child can make reliably for a morning injury.

q.young: Is your head hurting more each day?
q.older: Has your headache been getting stronger over the last few days?

candidates.why: A worsening trajectory over days is exactly what item 2 is for and what a repeat visit can capture.

q.young: Tell me how your head has felt today.
q.older: Tell me how your head has felt today compared with before.

candidates.why: When the child cannot place the injury in time, a spoken account lets the nurse reconstruct the trajectory instead of forcing a comparison the child cannot date.

q.young: Does your head hurt too much to play?
q.older: Is your headache stopping you doing things you would normally do?

candidates.why: A functional proxy for item 3 that avoids asking a child to rate a severity word; include only if the reviewer decides not to derive item 3 from the FPS-R screen.

q.young: Do you remember bumping your head?
q.older: Can you remember the moment you hit your head?

candidates.why: Item 4 is confirmed by two rules and is asked as whether they remember, never for how long the gap lasted.

q.young: Is there a bit you cannot remember?
q.older: Is there a part of what happened that you cannot remember at all?

candidates.why: Catches amnesia the child has noticed themselves without using the banned blackout phrasing or asking for a duration.

q.young: Tell me the last thing you remember before your head hurt.
q.older: Tell me the last thing you remember before you hit your head.

candidates.why: A spoken answer shows the nurse where the memory gap starts, which is more informative than a yes/no when the child is unsure of timing.

q.young: Did a grown-up say you would not wake up?
q.older: Did anyone tell you that you were not awake or not answering for a moment?

candidates.why: Item 5 is partial and CHALICE requires it witnessed, so the question asks what the child was told rather than treating their own account as fact.

q.young: Who was with you when it happened?
q.older: Who was with you when it happened, and what did they say afterwards?

candidates.why: Points the nurse at the person who could witness loss of consciousness, without asking the child to judge whether it happened.

q.young: Tell me how you hurt your head.
q.older: Tell me what you were doing when you hurt your head.

candidates.why: Item 6 has the child describe the event and the nurse classify it, so an open spoken answer beats any structured choice.

q.young: Did you fall off something? What was it?
q.older: If you fell, what did you fall from? For example the top bunk, a wall, or some stairs.

candidates.why: The three fall-height thresholds disagree, so the child names the object and the nurse maps it to whichever rule they use.

q.young: If you fell down stairs, how many steps?
q.older: If you fell down stairs, how many steps did you fall?

candidates.why: Stairs are the one height a child can count, and CATCH's five-stair criterion is stated in steps rather than metres.

q.young: Did something hit your head?
q.older: Did something hit your head, rather than you falling?

candidates.why: Separates a struck-by mechanism from a fall, which is the first split all three rules make before applying any threshold.

q.young: Did your arms or legs shake when you did not want them to?
q.older: After you hurt your head, did any part of your body shake or go stiff on its own?

candidates.why: Item 7 is mostly observer and must never be phrased as asking about a seizure, so it is described in body movements the child could notice.

q.young: Do you feel sleepy right now?
q.older: Do you feel more sleepy than you usually would at this time of day?

candidates.why: Item 13 is the child's own sense of sleepiness, not CHALICE's abnormal drowsiness; a no here is weak evidence and must not read as reassurance.

q.young: Was it hard to wake up this morning?
q.older: Was it harder than usual to wake up this morning?

candidates.why: A concrete moment the child can recall, which reports the same item 13 sleepiness without asking them to monitor their own drowsiness now.
